::: {#rem-score-name}
#### Why the score function is called "score"

The name comes from genetics.
@fisher1935linkage assigned each family in a study of linkage a "score",
which measured the family's evidence about the linkage parameter.
He compared that scoring rule with an "ideal score",
the derivative of the log of the sampling [density](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-pdf),
which is the [score](#def-score) function of these notes
[@wikipedia_informant_function]. <!-- check-term-links: allow -->
For [independent](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/independence.html#def-indpt) [observations](exploratory-descriptive.qmd#def-observation),
the [log-likelihood](#def-loglik) is a sum over observations,
so its derivative is also a sum, of one contribution per observation. <!-- check-term-links: allow -->
@rao1948large, who had worked on estimating linkage parameters in Fisher's genetics laboratory,
based a test on these "scores",
the derivatives of the log-likelihood,
and called it a score test [@bera2024score]. <!-- check-term-links: allow -->
The name then spread to the derivative itself.

In other settings, "score" means a different quantity.
These notes call a classifier's raw output the [log-odds](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-odds) or linear predictor, never a "score",
so that "score" always means the derivative of the log-likelihood. <!-- check-term-links: allow -->
:::
